semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {هُمَزَةٍ}: that is, one who does much hamz (backbiting by gesture or word); likewise «اللُّمَزَة» is one who does much lamz (slander). The meaning of hamz was treated in [Sūrat] Nūn, and lamz in [Sūrat] Barāʾa. The majority read the mīm with fatḥa, on the footing that what is meant is the person from whom that act is frequent. Ziyād al-Aʿjam said:
4640 - تُدْلِي بِوْدِّيْ إذا لا قَيْتَني كَذِباً ... وإنْ أُغَيَّبْ فأنتَ الهامِزُ اللُّمَزَةْ
(You offer me your friendship, falsely, when you meet me; and if I am absent, you are the backbiter, the slanderer.)
Al-Bāqir read with sukūn, meaning one at whom hamz and lamz are directed, that is, one who brings about what causes people to backbite and slander him, like «ḍuḥaka» for one who laughs much, and «ḍuḥka» for one at whom people laugh because of what he does. This is regular; I mean that the form fuʿala with fatḥa on the ʿayn is for one from whom the act is frequent, and with sukūn for one on account of whom the act occurs.

semin-durr:2-2.t:
His saying: {الذى جَمَعَ}: it may be put in the genitive as a badal (substitute), and in the accusative or the nominative by disjunction (qaṭʿ). It may not be put in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt) or an explicative apposition (bayān), because the two differ in definiteness and indefiniteness. As for His saying «جَمَعَ»: the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with shadda on the mīm, for intensity and multiplication, and because it agrees with «عَدَّدَه»; the others read «جمَعَ» without shadda, which admits both multiplication and its absence.
His saying «وعَدَّدَه»: the majority read it with the first dāl doubled, which is also for intensity. Al-Ḥasan and al-Kalbī read it without doubling. There are several views on it. The first: the meaning is "he gathered wealth and counted that wealth", that is, "and he gathered its number", that is, he reckoned it. The second: the meaning is "and he gathered the number of his own people from his clan and relatives". On these two interpretations «عَدَدَه» is a noun conjoined to «مالاً», that is, "and he gathered the number of the wealth" or "the number of his own people". The third: that «عَدَدَه» is a past verb meaning "he counted it" (ʿaddahu), except that it is irregular in being left unassimilated, as it is irregular in the saying:
4641 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ...
إني أَجُوْدُ لأَِقْوامٍ وإنْ ضَنِنُوا
(. . . I am generous to people, even if they are stingy.)

semin-durr:3-3.t: His saying: {يَحْسَبُ}: it may be resumptive (mustaʾnafa), and it may be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «جَمَعَ». As for «أَخْلَدَه», it means «يُخْلِدُه» ("will make him immortal"), the past having been put in the place of the imperfect. It was also said that it is in its original sense, that is: "it prolonged his life".

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {لَيُنبَذَنَّ}: the answer to an implied oath. ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Ḥasan (with a disagreement reported from him), Ibn Muḥayṣin and Abū ʿAmr in one report read «ليُنْبَذانِّ» with the alif of the dual, that is, "he and his wealth will both be cast". From al-Ḥasan also: «لَيُنْبَذُنَّ» with ḍamma on the dhāl, attributed to a plural pronoun, that is: "we shall surely cast the backbiter and his supporters".
Al-ḥuṭama is one who does much shattering (al-ḥaṭm). One says "a ḥuṭama man", that is, a glutton; and "ḥaṭamtuhu" means "I broke it"; and al-ḥuṭām (broken pieces) is from it. He said:
4642 - قد لَفَّها الليلُ بسَوَّاقٍ حُطَمْ
(Night has wrapped it up with a harsh, crushing driver.)
And another said:
4643 - إنَّا حَطَمْنا بالقضيبِ مُصْعَباً ... يومَ كسَرْنا أَنْفَه لِيَغْضَبا
(We smashed Muṣʿab with the rod, the day we broke his nose that he might be angered.)
His saying «نارُ الله»: that is, "it is the fire of Allah".

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {التي تَطَّلِعُ}: it may be a follower (tābiʿa) of «نارُ الله», and it may be disjoined (maqṭūʿa). . .

[Translator's note: the source entry breaks off here with an ellipsis; it is translated as it stands.]

semin-durr:9-9.t: His saying: {فِي عَمَدٍ}: the two brothers and Abū Bakr read it with two ḍammas, as the plural of «عَمُود» (column), like «rasūl» and «rusul». It was also said to be the plural of «ʿimād», like «kitāb» and «kutub». From Abū ʿAmr it is reported with ḍamma and sukūn, a lightening of this reading. The others read «عَمَد» with two fatḥas. It was said to be a collective noun (ism jamʿ) for «ʿamūd». It was also said that it is rather a plural of it; al-Farrāʾ said: like «adīm» and «adam». Abū ʿUbayda said: "It is the plural of «ʿimād»." «في عَمَدٍ» may be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in «عليهم», that is, "bound fast"; or the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, that is, "they are in columns"; or an attribute of «مُؤْصَدَة». Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "that is, the fire would then be inside the columns."
